questions.question: What are frozen string literals in Ruby?
questions.title: Frozen String Literals
questions.direct_answer: By default Ruby strings are mutable: `s = 'hi'; s << '!'` works. `# frozen_string_literal: true` (a magic comment at the top of a file) makes ALL string literals in that file immutable (frozen): `s = 'hi'; s << '!'` raises FrozenError. This prevents bugs (accidental mutation of shared strings) and improves performance (Ruby can share one copy, no allocation per literal). It's the modern default for new files. To mutate, build a new string (`s + '!'` returns a new one) or call `.dup` to get a mutable copy. The magic comment must be the first line (or after shebang/encoding). Per-file: each file needs its own. Strings from IO, +, gsub, etc. are NOT frozen by it (only literals). Use it in new code; in gems for thread-safety.

sections.title: Immutable by Default
sections.content: By default Ruby strings are mutable: s hi; s double-less-than exclamation works. frozen_string_literal true (a magic comment at the top of a file) makes ALL string literals in that file immutable (frozen): s hi; s double-less-than exclamation raises FrozenError. This prevents bugs (accidental mutation of shared strings) and improves performance (Ruby can share one copy, no allocation per literal). It's the modern default for new files. To mutate, build a new string (s plus exclamation returns a new one) or call dup to get a mutable copy. The magic comment must be the first line (or after shebang/encoding). Per-file: each file needs its own. Strings from IO, plus, gsub, etc. are NOT frozen by it (only literals). Use it in new code; in gems for thread-safety.

sections.title: Frozen String Literals
sections.content:
magic comment -> literals immutable. Prevents mutation bugs; improves perf. .dup to mutate.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M[# frozen_string_literal: true] --> F[all literals frozen]
  F --> S[s = 'hi'; s << '!' raises]
  F --> P[perf: shared one copy]
  M2[.dup] --> C[mutable copy]
```

sections.title: Frozen string literals
sections.content:
```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true   # <-- magic comment, FIRST line of the file

# After it, string LITERALS in this file are frozen:
s = 'hi'
s.frozen?         # true
# s << '!'        # raises FrozenError (can't mutate)
# s.upcase!       # raises FrozenError

# Build a NEW string instead (works fine):
s2 = s + '!'      # 'hi!' (new string, not frozen)
s2.frozen?        # false

# Or dup for a mutable copy:
s3 = s.dup        # mutable copy
s3 << '!'         # 'hi!' (works)

# NON-literal strings are NOT affected (only literals):
x = File.read('f.txt')   # not frozen (from IO)
y = 'a'.gsub('a', 'b')    # not frozen (from gsub)

# Per-file: each file needs its own comment (first line).
# Can be the 2nd line if a shebang/encoding is first:
#   #!/usr/bin/env ruby
#   # frozen_string_literal: true

# Use in new code (safety + perf); in gems for thread-safety.
# Mutation methods to watch: << , gsub!, upcase!, []=, replace.
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Trying to mutate a frozen literal (<< / gsub! raises FrozenError).
Expecting it to affect non-literal strings (only literals are frozen).
Forgetting it's per-file (each file needs its own comment).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: # frozen_string_literal: true (magic comment, top of file) makes string literals immutable.
It prevents accidental mutation of shared strings and improves performance (shared copy).
Mutating a frozen literal (<<, gsub!, upcase!) raises FrozenError.
To mutate: build a new string (s + '!') or .dup for a mutable copy.
Per-file (each file needs its own); only affects literals, not IO/+/gsub results.
